- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

4	programme. Derived from the existing TSD corpus in the SFCC Confluence space so a new TSD reads

10	| Template | Use when the TSD describes… | Modelled on |
11	| --- | --- | --- |
12	| [`tsd-integration-template.md`](./tsd-integration-template.md) | A **data domain or integration pipeline** — how data flows between systems, who owns it, and how it syncs. The most common kind. | Product · Price · Inventory · Orders · Catalogue Sync |
13	| [`tsd-architecture-template.md`](./tsd-architecture-template.md) | A **broad architectural foundation** spanning stack, multi-site, integrations, SSR/SEO, performance, testing, and CI/CD. Usually one per platform/programme. | Technical Solution Design – PWA |
14	| [`tsd-component-template.md`](./tsd-component-template.md) | A **buildable component, service, or agent** with defined component boundaries, credentials, and governance/guardrails. | AI-Assisted Defect Triage Agent |
15	
16	When a doc spans two genres (e.g. a component that is mostly an integration pipeline), start
17	from the closest-fit template and pull the extra sections you need from the others.
18	
19	## Conventions shared by all three
20	
21	These are the "TSD DNA" every existing Zimmermann TSD follows — the templates bake them in, but
22	keep them in mind while filling one out:
23	
24	1. **Open with boundaries.** State the system of record, the integration layer, and what each
25	   system does *not* do ("SFCC never connects to AP21 directly"). Ambiguity here is the most
26	   expensive kind.
27	2. **Say what's out of scope**, not just what's in — the broader the TSD, the more this matters.
28	3. **At least one diagram.** An ASCII data-flow / architecture sketch beats prose for boundaries.
29	   Link a Confluence whiteboard for anything richer.
30	4. **Tables are the default medium** — registers, mappings, endpoint lists, config.
31	5. **Capture the *why*, not just the *what*** — every TSD ends with a `Key Design Decisions`
32	   table (`Decision | Choice | Rationale`).
33	6. **Every unknown is a tracked open item** with an owner and a status — never a silent
34	   assumption. Mark inline unknowns `[TBC — owner]`.
35	7. **Trace to requirements / tickets** — reference functional-requirement IDs (`DMU-030`,
36	   `REG-041`, `PRC-34`, `CFD-023`) and JIRA keys (`SFCC-123`, `ZMOBLD-263`) wherever a claim maps
37	   to one.
38	8. **Cross-link related TSDs** rather than duplicating their content.
39	9. **Australian spelling** in Zimmermann-authored prose (`catalogue`, `colour`, `localisation`,
40	   `organisation`). Keep upstream Salesforce identifiers verbatim.
41	10. **Security where relevant** — never document a real secret; describe credential *boundaries*
42	    (where a token lives, what it can do, that it is never logged).
43	
44	## How to use
45	
46	1. Copy the chosen template to its home — a new Confluence page under

# TSD Templates

Templates for authoring a **Technical Solution Document (TSD)** for the Zimmermann SFCC / PWA
programme. Derived from the existing TSD corpus in the SFCC Confluence space so a new TSD reads
like the ones already signed off — same section order, same "why" tables, same open-items
discipline.

## Pick the right template

| Template | Use when the TSD describes… | Modelled on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`tsd-integration-template.md`](./tsd-integration-template.md) | A **data domain or integration pipeline** — how data flows between systems, who owns it, and how it syncs. The most common kind. | Product · Price · Inventory · Orders · Catalogue Sync |
| [`tsd-architecture-template.md`](./tsd-architecture-template.md) | A **broad architectural foundation** spanning stack, multi-site, integrations, SSR/SEO, performance, testing, and CI/CD. Usually one per platform/programme. | Technical Solution Design – PWA |
| [`tsd-component-template.md`](./tsd-component-template.md) | A **buildable component, service, or agent** with defined component boundaries, credentials, and governance/guardrails. | AI-Assisted Defect Triage Agent |

When a doc spans two genres (e.g. a component that is mostly an integration pipeline), start
from the closest-fit template and pull the extra sections you need from the others.

## Conventions shared by all three

These are the "TSD DNA" every existing Zimmermann TSD follows — the templates bake them in, but
keep them in mind while filling one out:

1. **Open with boundaries.** State the system of record, the integration layer, and what each
   system does *not* do ("SFCC never connects to AP21 directly"). Ambiguity here is the most
   expensive kind.
2. **Say what's out of scope**, not just what's in — the broader the TSD, the more this matters.
3. **At least one diagram.** An ASCII data-flow / architecture sketch beats prose for boundaries.
   Link a Confluence whiteboard for anything richer.
4. **Tables are the default medium** — registers, mappings, endpoint lists, config.
5. **Capture the *why*, not just the *what*** — every TSD ends with a `Key Design Decisions`
   table (`Decision | Choice | Rationale`).
6. **Every unknown is a tracked open item** with an owner and a status — never a silent
   assumption. Mark inline unknowns `[TBC — owner]`.
7. **Trace to requirements / tickets** — reference functional-requirement IDs (`DMU-030`,
   `REG-041`, `PRC-34`, `CFD-023`) and JIRA keys (`SFCC-123`, `ZMOBLD-263`) wherever a claim maps
   to one.
8. **Cross-link related TSDs** rather than duplicating their content.
9. **Australian spelling** in Zimmermann-authored prose (`catalogue`, `colour`, `localisation`,
   `organisation`). Keep upstream Salesforce identifiers verbatim.
10. **Security where relevant** — never document a real secret; describe credential *boundaries*
    (where a token lives, what it can do, that it is never logged).

## How to use

1. Copy the chosen template to its home — a new Confluence page under
   [05.1 — Architecture & Solution Design](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/277577731),
   or `.docs/` if it belongs in-repo.
2. Replace every `{{PLACEHOLDER}}`.
3. Delete `<!-- guidance -->` comments and any optional section that doesn't apply — an empty
   section is worse than no section.
4. Leave the `Open Items` table in place even at sign-off; a TSD with zero open items is rare and
   usually means something wasn't interrogated.

# CLAUDE.md — TelcoNow Customer Portal

> Source of truth for architecture, standards, and decisions. When silent, ask — never guess.

## Stack
| Concern | Choice | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Framework | Next.js 16 App Router | No Pages Router. Moved off 14 — EOL Oct 2025, carries a disclosed critical middleware-bypass CVE (CVSS 9.1) in the exact mechanism this project's auth depends on. Decided 2026-06-30. |
| Language | TypeScript strict | Zero `any`, no exceptions |
| Styling | Tailwind CSS | Mobile-first; token system; no arbitrary values without comment |
| Auth | Auth.js v5 (`next-auth`) | Credentials, JWT, email+password, stubbed |
| Data | Stub layer (`src/lib/stubs/`) | No CMS, no external API — stubs are production code |
| State | Zustand | Last resort: RSC→props→useState→context→Zustand |
| Testing | Vitest + RTL | TDD; all gates pass before PR |
| Deploy | Vercel | Edge Middleware enabled |

## Getting Started
**Requirements:** Node.js ≥ 20 (LTS) · pnpm ≥ 9

```bash
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # fill in AUTH_SECRET — see below
pnpm dev                     # http://localhost:3000
```

`.env.example` (commit this file — no secrets):
```
# Auth.js v5 — required
AUTH_SECRET=        # generate: openssl rand -base64 32
AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3000

1	# Zimmermann PWA Kit — Developer Onboarding & Ready-to-Work Checklist
2	
3	For every developer (either squad) joining the Zimmermann Salesforce PWA Kit build.
4	Work through this top to bottom — don't skip ahead. Check items off as you go, and
5	message the FED Lead if anything is blocked or unclear rather than guessing.
6	
7	_Compiled from the repo's `AGENTS.md`/`.claude/rules/` and a live scan of the Confluence
8	`SFCC` space on 2026-07-15 — Confluence access/status items may have moved on since;
9	re-check the linked pages rather than trusting this file as current forever._
10	
11	---
12	
13	## 1. Access & Accounts
14	
15	Check your own row on **[7.1a Tool Access Tracker](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/259686402)** first — as of the last scan, most non-lead developers show Jira/Confluence access as "Requested" (not yet confirmed). Chase Tash Lay if yours is still pending.
16	
17	- [ ] **Jira** access confirmed (request to: Natasha Lay)
18	- [ ] **Confluence** access confirmed (request to: Natasha Lay)
19	- [ ] **GitHub** org access confirmed — you can see `ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa` (request to: Mani)
20	- [ ] **Figma** access confirmed — both Accenture's instance and Zimmermann's instance if your role needs it (Accenture-owned)
21	- [ ] **SFCC Business Manager** access requested if your role needs it (request to: Mani)
22	- [ ] **SFCC MRT** access requested if your role needs it (request to: Mani)
23	- [ ] **Zephyr** access requested if you'll be writing/running E2E tests (needed for `/qa-generate` and BrowserStack story-scoped runs)
24	- [ ] **Magento** access requested if your role needs it (request to: Kim S) — note: 2FA issues are a known recurring blocker for this one, raise early
25	- [ ] **Contentful** access requested if your role touches CMS content types or components
26	- [ ] Full platform/tool ownership list: **[7.1 Platform and Tool Access](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/259358732)**
27	
28	**Contentful personal token** (only if your work touches Contentful):
29	- [ ] Generate your own personal CMA token: Contentful → top-right avatar → Account Settings → CMA Tokens → Create personal access token
30	- [ ] Add it to your local `.env` as `CONTENTFUL_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN` — **never** commit it, and never let it get pushed to the shared GitHub Environments (it's a `scope:personal` value, see `.env.sample`'s header)
31	- [ ] Reference: **[Contentful CMS — Setup & Operations](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/318472193)**
32	
33	---
34	
35	## 2. Machine & Codebase Setup
36	
37	Prerequisites: Node.js 18/20/22/24 LTS, npm 9+, Git, access to the Zimmermann GitHub org.
38	
39	```bash
40	git clone git@github.com:ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa.git
41	cd zimmermann-pwa
42	npm ci
43	```
44	- [ ] `npm ci` completed without errors
45	- [ ] Husky hooks installed automatically — verify with `ls .husky/` → should show `pre-commit commit-msg`. If missing (e.g. cloned with `--no-install`), install manually:
46	  ```bash
47	  cp scripts/hooks/pre-commit .git/hooks/pre-commit && chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
48	  cp scripts/hooks/commit-msg .git/hooks/commit-msg && chmod +x .git/hooks/commit-msg
49	  ```
50	- [ ] **Never bypass these hooks** with `git commit --no-verify`
51	
52	### Environment file setup
53	
54	> ⚠️ **Ignore the `cp .env.sample .env` instruction on the Confluence "Technical Environment
55	> Setup" page** — it's stale. The repo now uses a tiered `.env.shared` / `.env.<tier>` system.
56	> Use the real process below instead.
57	
58	```bash
59	npm run env -- init
60	```
61	- [ ] Ran `npm run env -- init` to scaffold `.env.shared` / `.env.<tier>`
62	- [ ] Filled in the values you were given by the Integration Lead (`COMMERCE_API_CLIENT_ID`, `COMMERCE_API_ORGANIZATION_ID`, `COMMERCE_API_SHORT_CODE`, `COMMERCE_API_SITE_ID`, Contentful tokens if applicable)
63	- [ ] Confirmed `.env*` files are gitignored — never commit them, never paste token values into `.env.sample`
64	- [ ] Full command reference: see `.env.sample`'s header comment in the repo
65	
66	### Start & verify
67	
68	```bash
69	npm start          # run in its own terminal — do not run inside a Claude Code session
70	npx tsc --noEmit    # TypeScript baseline should be clean
71	```
72	- [ ] `npm start` runs and `http://localhost:3000` loads locally
73	- [ ] `npx tsc --noEmit` passes with no errors
74	- [ ] `npm run lint` passes with no errors
75	
76	### Atlassian MCP (Jira/Confluence access from inside Claude)
77	
78	- [ ] Follow **[Claude Desktop — Atlassian MCP Setup Guide](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/275251202)** to connect Jira/Confluence via manual config — needs your own personal Atlassian API token, never a shared one
79	- [ ] Verified it works: ask Claude to look up a known Jira ticket or Confluence page and confirm it returns real data
80	
81	---
82	
83	## 3. Claude Code / AI Tooling Setup
84	
85	VSCode + Claude Code is the primary, recommended setup for this project — the rules, skills, and hooks are authored for it. Cursor and GitHub Copilot are also supported (rules are mirrored automatically via a sync script) if that's your preference.
86	
87	```bash
88	npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
89	claude login   # opens a browser — use your work email
90	claude --version
91	```
92	- [ ] Claude Code CLI installed and logged in with your **work email** (contact FED Lead if you don't have an Anthropic account yet)
93	- [ ] Ran a read-only first session to sanity check: open `claude` in the repo root and ask it to *"Describe the structure of this codebase without modifying any files."*
94	- [ ] Ran the **`/onboarding`** skill inside Claude Code — it asks your role, checks mechanical setup, and orients you to the rules/tools relevant to your role and squad
95	- [ ] Understand that **`/session-start`** must be run at the **start of every future session** — it reads project tracking docs, runs a health check, and states current position before any code gets written
96	- [ ] Understand the branching rule: `git branch --show-current` before doing anything — if it says `develop` or `main`, stop and create a feature branch first. **No exceptions, including under deadline pressure.**
97	- [ ] Understand `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is CI-automation-only — **never** use it on `release/**`, `develop`, or `main` in an interactive session
98	
99	If Claude Code ever modifies something it shouldn't have, the recovery steps are documented in the [Developer Onboarding Guide §7](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304775192) (stop session → `git diff --name-only` → revert Tier 1 changes → notify the file owner → refine your prompt).
100	
101	---
102	
103	## 4. Required Reading — Repo (read before writing any code)
104	
105	These are auto-loaded into every Claude Code session, but you should read them yourself too — they're the actual rulebook, not just AI config:
106	
107	- [ ] `AGENTS.md` — branch rules, hard rules, tier system, 4-step coding workflow, stop-and-ask matrix
108	- [ ] `.claude/rules/conventions.md` — cross-cutting naming/imports/DRY/security conventions
109	- [ ] `.claude/rules/typescript.md` — TS idioms used throughout `overrides/`
110	- [ ] `.claude/rules/css.md` — Chakra token usage, `.scss` conventions

116	- [ ] `.docs/memory/projectState.md` — what's live vs. mocked right now, current phase, in-progress work
117	- [ ] `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` — **check before scoping any new work** — don't build ahead of the current sprint
118	- [ ] `.docs/upstreamPolicy.md` — how/when the base `@salesforce/retail-react-app` template gets bumped
119	- [ ] `.docs/prd/index.md` and the PRD(s) for your squad's feature area(s) — see squad breakdown below
120	
121	---

124	
125	### Claude Code specific
126	- [ ] **[Claude Code CLI — Developer Onboarding Guide](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304775192)** — session rules, prompt-scoping worked examples, recovery steps

131	- [ ] **[Technical Solution Design – PWA](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/256835585)** — canonical architecture doc: integration boundaries, multi-site/session model, SSR vs. CSR per page type, env-var security table, Didomi consent-gate table
132	- [ ] **[Branching Guide (GitFlow)](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304840733)** — approval counts per branch, release tagging scripts

135	- [ ] **[04.2 Design Tracker](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/258801666)** — **check this before starting any UI work.** As of the last scan: Homepage, PLP core grid, global nav/footer, most PDP components, and Payments/Notify-Me CTAs are signed off. **Cart, Search, Checkout, Account, Wishlist, Gift Cards, Returns, Store Locator, and Z.immerse are still Draft/In Review** — not build-ready yet. This list moves — always re-check the live tracker, don't rely on this snapshot.

# Zimmermann PWA Kit — Developer Onboarding & Ready-to-Work Checklist

For every developer (either squad) joining the Zimmermann Salesforce PWA Kit build.
Work through this top to bottom — don't skip ahead. Check items off as you go, and
message the FED Lead if anything is blocked or unclear rather than guessing.

_Compiled from the repo's `AGENTS.md`/`.claude/rules/` and a live scan of the Confluence
`SFCC` space on 2026-07-15 — Confluence access/status items may have moved on since;
re-check the linked pages rather than trusting this file as current forever._

---

## 1. Access & Accounts

Check your own row on **[7.1a Tool Access Tracker](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/259686402)** first — as of the last scan, most non-lead developers show Jira/Confluence access as "Requested" (not yet confirmed). Chase Tash Lay if yours is still pending.

- [ ] **Jira** access confirmed (request to: Natasha Lay)
- [ ] **Confluence** access confirmed (request to: Natasha Lay)
- [ ] **GitHub** org access confirmed — you can see `ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa` (request to: Mani)
- [ ] **Figma** access confirmed — both Accenture's instance and Zimmermann's instance if your role needs it (Accenture-owned)
- [ ] **SFCC Business Manager** access requested if your role needs it (request to: Mani)
- [ ] **SFCC MRT** access requested if your role needs it (request to: Mani)
- [ ] **Zephyr** access requested if you'll be writing/running E2E tests (needed for `/qa-generate` and BrowserStack story-scoped runs)
- [ ] **Magento** access requested if your role needs it (request to: Kim S) — note: 2FA issues are a known recurring blocker for this one, raise early
- [ ] **Contentful** access requested if your role touches CMS content types or components
- [ ] Full platform/tool ownership list: **[7.1 Platform and Tool Access](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/259358732)**

**Contentful personal token** (only if your work touches Contentful):
- [ ] Generate your own personal CMA token: Contentful → top-right avatar → Account Settings → CMA Tokens → Create personal access token
- [ ] Add it to your local `.env` as `CONTENTFUL_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN` — **never** commit it, and never let it get pushed to the shared GitHub Environments (it's a `scope:personal` value, see `.env.sample`'s header)
- [ ] Reference: **[Contentful CMS — Setup & Operations](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/318472193)**

---

## 2. Machine & Codebase Setup

Prerequisites: Node.js 18/20/22/24 LTS, npm 9+, Git, access to the Zimmermann GitHub org.

```bash
git clone git@github.com:ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa.git
cd zimmermann-pwa
npm ci
```
- [ ] `npm ci` completed without errors
- [ ] Husky hooks installed automatically — verify with `ls .husky/` → should show `pre-commit commit-msg`. If missing (e.g. cloned with `--no-install`), install manually:
  ```bash
  cp scripts/hooks/pre-commit .git/hooks/pre-commit && chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
  cp scripts/hooks/commit-msg .git/hooks/commit-msg && chmod +x .git/hooks/commit-msg
  ```
- [ ] **Never bypass these hooks** with `git commit --no-verify`

### Environment file setup

> ⚠️ **Ignore the `cp .env.sample .env` instruction on the Confluence "Technical Environment
> Setup" page** — it's stale. The repo now uses a tiered `.env.shared` / `.env.<tier>` system.
> Use the real process below instead.

```bash
npm run env -- init
```
- [ ] Ran `npm run env -- init` to scaffold `.env.shared` / `.env.<tier>`
- [ ] Filled in the values you were given by the Integration Lead (`COMMERCE_API_CLIENT_ID`, `COMMERCE_API_ORGANIZATION_ID`, `COMMERCE_API_SHORT_CODE`, `COMMERCE_API_SITE_ID`, Contentful tokens if applicable)
- [ ] Confirmed `.env*` files are gitignored — never commit them, never paste token values into `.env.sample`
- [ ] Full command reference: see `.env.sample`'s header comment in the repo

### Start & verify

```bash
npm start          # run in its own terminal — do not run inside a Claude Code session
npx tsc --noEmit    # TypeScript baseline should be clean
```
- [ ] `npm start` runs and `http://localhost:3000` loads locally
- [ ] `npx tsc --noEmit` passes with no errors
- [ ] `npm run lint` passes with no errors

### Atlassian MCP (Jira/Confluence access from inside Claude)

- [ ] Follow **[Claude Desktop — Atlassian MCP Setup Guide](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/275251202)** to connect Jira/Confluence via manual config — needs your own personal Atlassian API token, never a shared one
- [ ] Verified it works: ask Claude to look up a known Jira ticket or Confluence page and confirm it returns real data

---

## 3. Claude Code / AI Tooling Setup

VSCode + Claude Code is the primary, recommended setup for this project — the rules, skills, and hooks are authored for it. Cursor and GitHub Copilot are also supported (rules are mirrored automatically via a sync script) if that's your preference.

```bash
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
claude login   # opens a browser — use your work email
claude --version
```
- [ ] Claude Code CLI installed and logged in with your **work email** (contact FED Lead if you don't have an Anthropic account yet)
- [ ] Ran a read-only first session to sanity check: open `claude` in the repo root and ask it to *"Describe the structure of this codebase without modifying any files."*
- [ ] Ran the **`/onboarding`** skill inside Claude Code — it asks your role, checks mechanical setup, and orients you to the rules/tools relevant to your role and squad
- [ ] Understand that **`/session-start`** must be run at the **start of every future session** — it reads project tracking docs, runs a health check, and states current position before any code gets written
- [ ] Understand the branching rule: `git branch --show-current` before doing anything — if it says `develop` or `main`, stop and create a feature branch first. **No exceptions, including under deadline pressure.**
- [ ] Understand `--dangerously-skip-permissions` is CI-automation-only — **never** use it on `release/**`, `develop`, or `main` in an interactive session

If Claude Code ever modifies something it shouldn't have, the recovery steps are documented in the [Developer Onboarding Guide §7](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304775192) (stop session → `git diff --name-only` → revert Tier 1 changes → notify the file owner → refine your prompt).

---

## 4. Required Reading — Repo (read before writing any code)

These are auto-loaded into every Claude Code session, but you should read them yourself too — they're the actual rulebook, not just AI config:

- [ ] `AGENTS.md` — branch rules, hard rules, tier system, 4-step coding workflow, stop-and-ask matrix
- [ ] `.claude/rules/conventions.md` — cross-cutting naming/imports/DRY/security conventions
- [ ] `.claude/rules/typescript.md` — TS idioms used throughout `overrides/`
- [ ] `.claude/rules/css.md` — Chakra token usage, `.scss` conventions
- [ ] `.claude/rules/components.md` — component/hook structure, Storybook categorisation
- [ ] `.claude/rules/testing.md` — Vitest / Storybook `play` / Playwright layer selection
- [ ] `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md` — **Tier 1**, frozen files (know these before you touch anything)
- [ ] `.claude/rules/protectedFiles.md` — **Tier 2**, protected files (need second-reviewer approval)
- [ ] `.docs/architecture.md` — stack overview, overrides pattern, path aliases, component organisation
- [ ] `.docs/memory/projectState.md` — what's live vs. mocked right now, current phase, in-progress work
- [ ] `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` — **check before scoping any new work** — don't build ahead of the current sprint
- [ ] `.docs/upstreamPolicy.md` — how/when the base `@salesforce/retail-react-app` template gets bumped
- [ ] `.docs/prd/index.md` and the PRD(s) for your squad's feature area(s) — see squad breakdown below

---

## 5. Required Reading — Confluence (direct links)

### Claude Code specific
- [ ] **[Claude Code CLI — Developer Onboarding Guide](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304775192)** — session rules, prompt-scoping worked examples, recovery steps
- [ ] **[Claude Code Skills Reference](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/297959425)** — what each custom skill does
- [ ] **[1.2 Team Overview](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/261586947)** — who's who, who to contact for what

### Architecture & process
- [ ] **[Technical Solution Design – PWA](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/256835585)** — canonical architecture doc: integration boundaries, multi-site/session model, SSR vs. CSR per page type, env-var security table, Didomi consent-gate table
- [ ] **[Branching Guide (GitFlow)](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304840733)** — approval counts per branch, release tagging scripts
- [ ] **[PWA CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions)](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/305561601)**
- [ ] **[SIT Quality Gates](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/304840754)** — thresholds & required secrets
- [ ] **[04.2 Design Tracker](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/258801666)** — **check this before starting any UI work.** As of the last scan: Homepage, PLP core grid, global nav/footer, most PDP components, and Payments/Notify-Me CTAs are signed off. **Cart, Search, Checkout, Account, Wishlist, Gift Cards, Returns, Store Locator, and Z.immerse are still Draft/In Review** — not build-ready yet. This list moves — always re-check the live tracker, don't rely on this snapshot.

### AI-Assisted QA pipeline (if you'll be writing E2E coverage)
- [ ] **[AI-Assisted QA — six-stage pipeline overview](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/277544962)** (Story → AC → Zephyr → Playwright → BrowserStack → Triage), plus Guides 1–4 linked from that page

---

## 6. Squad Context — pick what applies to you

Squad ownership (per `AGENTS.md`): **Squad A** owns checkout/cart/payments; **Squad B** owns PDP/PLP/search/account. Message the *other* squad's lead before touching their territory — even from within your own squad's area, if it overlaps.

# TSD Templates

Templates for authoring a **Technical Solution Document (TSD)** for the Zimmermann SFCC / PWA
programme. Derived from the existing TSD corpus in the SFCC Confluence space so a new TSD reads
like the ones already signed off — same section order, same "why" tables, same open-items
discipline.

## Pick the right template

| Template | Use when the TSD describes… | Modelled on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`tsd-integration-template.md`](./tsd-integration-template.md) | A **data domain or integration pipeline** — how data flows between systems, who owns it, and how it syncs. The most common kind. | Product · Price · Inventory · Orders · Catalogue Sync |
| [`tsd-architecture-template.md`](./tsd-architecture-template.md) | A **broad architectural foundation** spanning stack, multi-site, integrations, SSR/SEO, performance, testing, and CI/CD. Usually one per platform/programme. | Technical Solution Design – PWA |
| [`tsd-component-template.md`](./tsd-component-template.md) | A **buildable component, service, or agent** with defined component boundaries, credentials, and governance/guardrails. | AI-Assisted Defect Triage Agent |

When a doc spans two genres (e.g. a component that is mostly an integration pipeline), start
from the closest-fit template and pull the extra sections you need from the others.

## Conventions shared by all three

These are the "TSD DNA" every existing Zimmermann TSD follows — the templates bake them in, but
keep them in mind while filling one out:

1. **Open with boundaries.** State the system of record, the integration layer, and what each
   system does *not* do ("SFCC never connects to AP21 directly"). Ambiguity here is the most
   expensive kind.
2. **Say what's out of scope**, not just what's in — the broader the TSD, the more this matters.
3. **At least one diagram.** An ASCII data-flow / architecture sketch beats prose for boundaries.
   Link a Confluence whiteboard for anything richer.
4. **Tables are the default medium** — registers, mappings, endpoint lists, config.
5. **Capture the *why*, not just the *what*** — every TSD ends with a `Key Design Decisions`
   table (`Decision | Choice | Rationale`).
6. **Every unknown is a tracked open item** with an owner and a status — never a silent
   assumption. Mark inline unknowns `[TBC — owner]`.
7. **Trace to requirements / tickets** — reference functional-requirement IDs (`DMU-030`,
   `REG-041`, `PRC-34`, `CFD-023`) and JIRA keys (`SFCC-123`, `ZMOBLD-263`) wherever a claim maps
   to one.
8. **Cross-link related TSDs** rather than duplicating their content.
9. **Australian spelling** in Zimmermann-authored prose (`catalogue`, `colour`, `localisation`,
   `organisation`). Keep upstream Salesforce identifiers verbatim.
10. **Security where relevant** — never document a real secret; describe credential *boundaries*
    (where a token lives, what it can do, that it is never logged).

## How to use

1. Copy the chosen template to its home — a new Confluence page under
   [05.1 — Architecture & Solution Design](https://zimmermannworkboard.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/SFCC/pages/277577731),
   or `.docs/` if it belongs in-repo.
2. Replace every `{{PLACEHOLDER}}`.
3. Delete `<!-- guidance -->` comments and any optional section that doesn't apply — an empty
   section is worse than no section.
4. Leave the `Open Items` table in place even at sign-off; a TSD with zero open items is rare and
   usually means something wasn't interrogated.

1	# Talking Points — Engineering Harnesses & Guardrails
2	_For: presenting to Accenture's Innovation Lead (Managing Director)_
3	_Pair with: `zimmermann-pwa-guardrails-tree.md` — same 12 sections, same order, so you can move through both side by side._
4	
5	---
6	
7	## Opening — set the frame
8	
9	> "You asked what engineering harnesses and guardrails we have in place on this build, so I want to
10	> walk you through where things actually stand — this is what we've put together so far, not a finished
11	> system. I'll go through it in the same order as the diagram I've shared, roughly following how a change
12	> moves from a developer's — or an AI agent's — hands into production. Some of this is solid, some of it
13	> we're still hardening, and I'd rather be upfront about both."
14	
15	---
16	
17	## The walkthrough (12 points, same order as the diagram)
18	
19	**§1 — Branch & Merge Guardrails**
20	> "Feature work happens on its own branch, never straight on the branch that goes live. The closer a
21	> branch is to production, the more sign-off it needs to merge."
22	
23	**§2 — File Protection Tiers**
24	> "Files are grouped roughly by how much damage a mistake could do — a homepage tweak is treated
25	> differently to a change touching payments or design tokens. The higher tiers need a named approver.
26	> It's not a perfect system, but it's meant to take 'did anyone notice this was sensitive' out of memory."
27	
28	**§3 — CI/CD Pipeline**
29	> "Before a person reviews a change, it's already run through automated tests, an accessibility check,
30	> and a performance budget. Worth flagging: one of those checks — a contract test with a partner API —
31	> is still a placeholder today, so I don't want to overstate that one."
32	
33	**§4 — AI PR Review Tooling**
34	> "An AI review tool also looks at every pull request, checking for a handful of specific things like
35	> exposed secrets or unsafe HTML. It's an extra pair of eyes, not a replacement for the human review that
36	> still happens after it."
37	
38	**§5 — Git Hooks**
39	> "Before a commit even leaves someone's laptop, it's checked for things like accidentally-committed
40	> secrets and commit message formatting. Small and unglamorous, but it catches mistakes early and cheaply."
41	
42	**§6 — Claude Code Session Harness**
43	> "We're using Claude Code, an AI coding agent, on parts of this build. It's mechanically prevented from
44	> writing to production branches, not just told not to, and it inherits the same file-ownership tiers a
45	> person would. This is newer territory for us, and we're still learning where the edges of it are."
46	
47	**§7 — TypeScript / Lint / Build Enforcement**
48	> "Type checking and lint rules catch a class of mistakes before code even runs. Not everything here is
49	> a hard block yet — some of it is still a warning rather than something that stops a merge."
50	
51	**§8 — Test Harness**
52	> "Unit tests, component-level tests, and end-to-end browser tests each cover a different layer, so we're
53	> not leaning on one kind of test to catch everything."
54	
55	**§9 — Environment, Secrets & Deployment Gates**
56	> "Credentials are scoped by environment, and promoting to each environment needs the right person's
57	> sign-off. Nothing clever here — just trying to keep it boring and consistent."
58	
59	**§10 — Contentful Sync Safety**
60	> "Our content syncing only ever adds fields, never removes them, so a bad push can't silently delete
61	> something that's live."
62	
63	**§11 — AI-Assisted QA Six-Stage Pipeline**
64	> "Separately, there's a QA process where AI helps draft acceptance criteria and test cases — but a
65	> person signs off at three separate points before any of it goes further. This one lives more in our
66	> process documentation than in the codebase itself, so I'd treat it as a work-in-progress alongside
67	> everything else."
68	
69	**§12 — Security & Privacy Boundaries**
70	> "Third-party scripts wait for a customer's consent before loading, and we've tried to limit how much
71	> damage one integration failing could do to the rest of the site. Also mostly a documentation-level
72	> guardrail — we didn't re-verify every part of the implementation for this walkthrough."
73	
74	---
75	
76	## Closing — the takeaway
77	
78	> "So that's roughly where we are, section by section: explicit rather than assumed ownership, some
79	> automated checks ahead of human review, an attempt to constrain the AI agent the same way we'd
80	> constrain a person, and a human decision point that doesn't get skipped. It's not complete, and I'd
81	> rather tell you what's still rough than gloss over it. If parts of this turn out useful beyond this
82	> account, that'd be a nice outcome, but it's early to claim that — right now it's just what we've built
83	> for this one."
84	
85	---
86	
87	## Q&A soundbites (if pushed on specifics)
88	
89	- **"What stops the AI from just breaking something in production?"**
90	  → "It can't write to a production branch — that's a mechanical block, not just an instruction. I
91	  wouldn't call it bulletproof, but it's a real constraint, not a policy on paper."
92	
93	- **"Is this mature, or held together with tape?"**
94	  → "Somewhere in between. We reviewed it ourselves and found a couple of gaps — one CI check is a
95	  placeholder, one approval step is enforced by process rather than code. We'd rather surface that
96	  ourselves than have it found later."
97	
98	- **"Does this slow the team down?"**
99	  → "Some overhead, but a lot of it replaces manual review time rather than adding to it. I don't have
100	  hard numbers on the net effect yet."
101	
102	- **"Could we reuse this on another account?"**
103	  → "Possibly, in shape if not in specifics — but we haven't tried transplanting it anywhere else, so
104	  I'd treat that as a hope rather than a proven claim."
105

**§12 — Security & Privacy Boundaries**
> "Third-party scripts wait for a customer's consent before loading, and we've tried to limit how much
> damage one integration failing could do to the rest of the site. Also mostly a documentation-level
> guardrail — we didn't re-verify every part of the implementation for this walkthrough."

---

## Closing — the takeaway

> "So that's roughly where we are, section by section: explicit rather than assumed ownership, some
> automated checks ahead of human review, an attempt to constrain the AI agent the same way we'd
> constrain a person, and a human decision point that doesn't get skipped. It's not complete, and I'd
> rather tell you what's still rough than gloss over it. If parts of this turn out useful beyond this
> account, that'd be a nice outcome, but it's early to claim that — right now it's just what we've built
> for this one."

---

## Q&A soundbites (if pushed on specifics)

- **"What stops the AI from just breaking something in production?"**
  → "It can't write to a production branch — that's a mechanical block, not just an instruction. I
  wouldn't call it bulletproof, but it's a real constraint, not a policy on paper."

- **"Is this mature, or held together with tape?"**
  → "Somewhere in between. We reviewed it ourselves and found a couple of gaps — one CI check is a
  placeholder, one approval step is enforced by process rather than code. We'd rather surface that
  ourselves than have it found later."

- **"Does this slow the team down?"**
  → "Some overhead, but a lot of it replaces manual review time rather than adding to it. I don't have
  hard numbers on the net effect yet."

- **"Could we reuse this on another account?"**
  → "Possibly, in shape if not in specifics — but we haven't tried transplanting it anywhere else, so
  I'd treat that as a hope rather than a proven claim."

│   ├── Guardrails/              4 files (guardrails + source-map + tree + presentation-script)
